column4: AlphaQubit: Google’s research on quantum error correction
column5: AlphaQubit: Google’s research on quantum error correction AlphaQubit tackles one of quantum computing’s biggest challenges Nov 20, 2024 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Our new AI system accurately identifies errors inside quantum computers, helping to make this new technology more reliable. Google DeepMind and Quantum AI teams Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Quantum computers have the potential to revolutionize drug discovery, material design and fundamental physics — that is, if we can get them to work reliably. Certain problems, which would take a conventional computer billions of years to solve, would take a quantum computer just hours. However, these new processors are more prone to noise than conventional ones. If we want to make quantum computers more reliable, especially at scale, we need to accurately identify and correct these errors. In a paper published today in Nature , we introduce AlphaQubit, an AI-based decoder that identifies quantum computing errors with state-of-the-art accuracy. This collaborative work brought together Google DeepMind’s machine learning knowledge and Google Quantum AI’s error correction expertise to accelerate progress on building a reliable quantum computer. Accurately identifying errors is a critical step towards making quantum computers capable of performing long computations at scale, opening the doors to scientific breakthroughs and many new areas of discovery. Related Article What is quantum computing? Learn more in our Ask a Techspert series. See more Correcting quantum computing errors Quantum computers harness the unique properties of matter at the smallest scales, such as superposition and entanglement, to solve certain types of complex problems in far fewer steps than classical computers. The technology relies on qubits, or quantum bits, which can sift through vast sets of possibilities using quantum interference to find an answer. The natural quantum state of a qubit is fragile and can be disrupted by various factors: microscopic defects in hardware, heat, vibration, electromagnetic interference and even cosmic rays (which are everywhere). Quantum error correction offers a way forward by using redundancy: grouping multiple qubits into a single logical qubit, and regularly performing consistency checks on it. The decoder preserves quantum information by using these consistency checks to identify errors in the logical qubit, so they can be corrected. Here, we illustrate how nine physical qubits (small gray circles) in a qubit grid of side length 3 (code distance) form a logical qubit. At each step, 8 more qubits perform consistency checks (square and semicircle areas, blue and magenta when failing and gray otherwise) at each time step which inform the neural network decoder (AlphaQubit). At the end of the experiment, AlphaQubit determines what errors occurred. Creating a neural-network contender for decoding AlphaQubit is a neural-network based decoder drawing on Transformers , a deep learning architecture developed at Google that underpins many of today’s large language models. Using the consistency checks as an input, its task is to correctly predict whether the logical qubit — when measured at the end of the experiment — has flipped from how it was prepared. We began by training our model to decode the data from a set of 49 qubits inside a Sycamore quantum processor , the central computational unit of the quantum computer. To teach AlphaQubit the general decoding problem, we used a quantum simulator to generate hundreds of millions of examples across a variety of settings and error levels. Then we finetuned AlphaQubit for a specific decoding task by giving it thousands of experimental samples from a particular Sycamore processor. When tested on new Sycamore data, AlphaQubit set a new standard for accuracy when compared with the previous leading decoders. In the largest Sycamore experiments, AlphaQubit makes 6% fewer errors than tensor network methods, which are highly accurate but impractically slow . AlphaQubit also makes 30% fewer errors than correlated matching , an accurate decoder that is fast enough to scale. Decoding accuracies for small and large Sycamore experiments (distance 3 = 17 physical qubits, and distance 5 = 49 physical qubits). AlphaQubit is more accurate than the tensor network (TN, a method that is not expected to scale at large experiments) and correlated matching (an accurate decoder with the speed to scale). Scaling AlphaQubit for future systems We expect quantum computers to advance beyond what’s available today. To see how AlphaQubit would adapt to larger devices with lower error levels, we trained it using data from simulated quantum systems of up to 241 qubits, as this exceeded what was available on the Sycamore platform. Again, AlphaQubit outperformed leading algorithmic decoders, suggesting it will also work on mid-sized quantum devices in the future. Decoding accuracies for different scaling/simulated experiments, from distance 3 (17 qubits) to distance 11 (241 qubits). The Tensor Network decoder does not appear in this graph, as it is too slow to run at large distances. The accuracy of the other two decoders increases when increasing distance (that is, when using more physical qubits). At each distance, AlphaQubit is more accurate than correlated matching. Our system also demonstrated advanced features like the ability to accept and report confidence levels on inputs and outputs. These information-rich interfaces can help further improve the performance of the quantum processor. And when we trained AlphaQubit on samples that included up to 25 rounds of error correction, it maintained good performance on simulated experiments of up to 100,000 rounds, showing its ability to generalize to scenarios beyond its training data. Moving towards practical quantum computing AlphaQubit represents a major milestone in using machine learning for quantum error correction. But we still face significant challenges involving speed and scalability. For example, each consistency check in a fast superconducting quantum processor is measured a million times every second. While AlphaQubit is great at accurately identifying errors, it’s still too slow to correct errors in a superconducting processor in real time. As quantum computing grows toward the potentially millions of qubits needed for commercially relevant applications, we’ll also need to find more data-efficient ways of training AI-based decoders. Our teams are combining pioneering advances in machine learning and quantum error correction to overcome these challenges — and pave the way for reliable quantum computers that can tackle some of the world’s most complex problems. Two families of non-axisymmetric solutions were recently discovered by Landreman [ arXiv:2609.26742 ] as counterexamples to Grad's conjecture, but both satisfy stellarator symmetry. Here, we generalize both families by introducing a symmetry-breaking parameter into each of the solutions, resulting in new non-axisymmetric solutions that break stellarator symmetry and reduce to the stellarator symmetric solutions when the newly introduced parameter is set to zero. column4: Bringing Expert Genome Interpretation to Every NICU | Gamow Labs
column5: Bringing Expert Genome Interpretation to Every NICU | Gamow Labs October 13, 2026 · Daniel McKinnon Bringing Expert Genome Interpretation to Every NICU For the Frost family, an unexplained loss left a question about their future. A new look at their son’s genome helped bring an answer. The Frost family today, with the son they welcomed through IVF. 01 / The family A family searching for answers The Frost family knew they wanted to grow their family, but, due to their unfortunate circumstances, were unsure that they could safely do so. Three years ago, they lost their infant son in the NICU due to an unexplained lung disease. His genome had been sequenced. Clinical lab specialists reviewed the results. The case was eventually referred to one of the world’s leading experts in rare developmental lung disorders. Sadly, the answers they were searching for never came. Without a diagnosis, the parents had no way of knowing whether their son’s illness had been a random, singular tragedy or something hidden within their own DNA that could happen again. They turned to IVF, hoping genetic testing could reduce that risk, but without a known mutation to test for, the best decision they could make was with incomplete information. In a research study with Baylor College of Medicine, Gamow Labs researchers reanalyzed the genome using an AI tool. They found a hidden genetic clue that clinicians confirmed for their diagnosis. 02 / The challenge Genome sequencing often represents hope. Today, patients in the NICU that are critically ill can have their entire genome sequenced in a matter of days. But translating the three billion letters into an explanation for why a child is suffering, and giving families actionable information, remains out of reach for many. Access to expertise Genome interpretation requires resources that not all NICUs have. A baby born in a lower-level unit may need a formal consult, a telehealth referral, or a transfer to another hospital before the right specialist ever sees them. Time to an answer With the right team in place, interpretation takes time, and manual reviews can fail to diagnose. A 2023 study of the country's top-tier NICU network found that even those best-resourced hospitals often couldn't get comprehensive genetic testing back fast enough to shape urgent treatment decisions. Science that keeps moving The science is also constantly evolving. Every month, researchers discover new disease genes, classify new variants, and publish new papers. These discoveries rarely make their way back to patients whose resolution had been inconclusive years prior. All of these factors culminate in families not having answers when they need them. At Gamow Labs, our hypothesis is straightforward: properly designed AI agents can help clinicians and researchers analyze genomes faster, more consistently, and at a scale that would be impossible through manual review alone. We are not in the business of replacing geneticists. We want to make expert-level genomic interpretation available to every family, regardless of where they receive care. 03 / The study Testing George on 26 challenging cases To test whether that vision could work in practice, we partnered with Dr. Pawel Stankiewicz at Baylor College of Medicine, one of the world's leading experts in developmental lung disorders. In a blinded study, his team provided deidentified whole genome sequences from 26 infants with interstitial lung disease whose diagnoses had been missed by first-line clinical laboratories and were then escalated to Dr. Stankiewicz. Dr. Stankiewicz’s lab subsequently solved 19/26, leaving 7 as mysteries. Study at a glance A new look at the same 26 genomes Each square represents one case in the blinded cohort. 19 Previous findings reproduced Cases already solved by Dr. Stankiewicz's lab 7 Previously unsolved cases Two additional candidates identified for validation 19 reproduced 2 new candidates 5 remaining cases “These are some of the most challenging cases in genomic medicine,” said Dr. Stankiewicz. “The patients had already undergone genome sequencing and clinical review, yet their diagnoses remained elusive. Solving these cases often requires looking beyond the standard ways of analyzing a genome and considering evidence from across the genome and the scientific literature.” Routine clinical software can only screen for expected patterns. With George-0.1, our research pipeline using frontier models like Gemini 4 Argon, our researchers cross-referenced raw sequencing data against medical papers. This helped surface candidate variants and supporting evidence for clinicians to review. Specialized agents examine different forms of evidence, search the literature, and assemble candidate molecular findings supported by traceable evidence for clinical review. Using this tool across the blinded study, our researchers matched the previously solved 19 cases. They also flagged candidate variants in 2 unsolved cases for Dr. Stankiewicz’s lab to validate. The Frost family's son was one of those two. 04 / The finding Finding the hidden rearrangement We found clusters of discordant read pairs along with split reads spanning the predicted breakpoint junctions, suggesting a balanced translocation in Baby Frost’s genome: a rearrangement in which a piece of DNA breaks off and reattaches somewhere else. In this case, this rearrangement would separate the FOXF1 enhancer from the FOXF1 gene, which would reduce FOXF1 expression to a lethal level and support the previous diagnosis of alveolar capillary dysplasia (ACD), a rare developmental disorder that prevents a newborn's lungs from supplying oxygen to the body. Understanding the finding A balanced translocation exchanges chromosome segments 01 Before the exchange The enhancer and FOXF1 gene start on the same chromosome, on opposite sides of the breakpoint. Dashed lines mark the breaks. 02 After the exchange The enhancer stays on derivative A. The FOXF1 gene moves with segment A2 to derivative B, separating the gene from its enhancer. Because this kind of evidence can be artifactual in short-read whole genome sequencing, this hypothesis was confirmed with Sanger sequencing in Dr. Stankiewicz’s lab. After confirmation, the case was considered solved. Using Argon, researchers also identified why routine clinical software missed this rearrangement for so long; among other issues, annotation bugs mistakenly flagged it as common and filtered it out. 05 / The answer What an answer meant for the Frost family After validating our findings, Dr. Stankiewicz shared, “I think the most exciting possibility is that tools like this could give clinicians a faster path to genomic interpretation. For critically ill newborns, time matters. Access to our expertise can be limited. So having that capability available at scale could be a major shift for neonatal medicine.” Dr. Stankiewicz confirmed the findings and shared his diagnosis with the Frost family. “This information was an incredible gift,” said Randall Frost. “It didn’t undo our loss, but it gave my wife and I closure and the confidence to move forward in growing our family.” We hope that delivering answers to the Frost family is just the beginning. Previous work has shown that re-analysis like this consistently reveals new diagnoses due to better tools, models, and science, and scaled AI-based approaches make this easier than ever before. This evaluation benhchmark covers a variety of topics related to spatial reasoning and world knowledge focused on real-world scenarios, particularly in the context of robotics. Please find more details and visualizations in the tech report . ERQA Dataset The questions consist of multimodal interleaved images and text, phrased as multiple-choice questions. The answers are provided as a single letter (A, B, C, D) for each question. We provide the ERQA benchmark in data/erqa.tfrecord as TF Examples saved with the following features: question : The text question to ask image/encoded : One or more encoded images answer : The ground truth answer question_type : The type of question (optional) visual_indices : Indices of visual elements (determines image placement) Setup Instructions 1. Install Dependencies Once the virtual environment is activated, install the required packages: pip install -r requirements.txt 2. Run example dataset loader To see the structure of the ERQA dataset and how to load examples from the TFRecord file, run the simple dataset loader: python loading_example.py This script demonstrates how to: Load the TFRecord file Parse examples with their features (questions, images, answers, etc.) Access the data in each example Handle the visual indices that determine image placement Multimodal Evaluation Harness We also provide an example of a lightweight evaluation harness for querying multimodal APIs (Gemini 2.0 and OpenAI) with examples loaded from the ERQA benchmark. Setup Install the required dependencies: pip install -r requirements.txt Set up your API keys. You can easily register a new Gemini API key here . API Key Configuration There are multiple ways to provide API keys to the evaluation harness: Option 1: Environment Variables Set environment variables for the APIs you want to use: # For Gemini API export GEMINI_API_KEY= " your_gemini_api_key_here " # For OpenAI API export OPENAI_API_KEY= " your_openai_api_key_here " Option 2: Command-line Arguments Provide API keys directly as command-line arguments: # For a single Gemini API key python eval_harness.py --gemini_api_key YOUR_GEMINI_API_KEY # For a single OpenAI API key python eval_harness.py --api openai --openai_api_key YOUR_OPENAI_API_KEY Option 3: API Keys File Create a text file with your API keys and provide the path to the file. This is helpful when you have multiple API keys for the same API and are running into rate limits per key. # Using a keys file python eval_harness.py --api_keys_file path/to/your/keys.txt The keys file should have one key per line, the keys will be assumed to be for the API specified with the --api argument. YOUR_API_KEY_1 YOUR_API_KEY_2 Running the Evaluation Harness Basic Usage Run the evaluation harness with default settings (Gemini API): python eval_harness.py Specifying a Model For Gemini API: # Using the default Gemini Flash model python eval_harness.py --model gemini-2.0-flash # Using the experimental Gemini Pro model python eval_harness.py --model gemini-2.0-pro-exp-02-05 For OpenAI API: # Using the GPT-4o-mini model python eval_harness.py --api openai --model gpt-4o-2024-11-20 Setting the Number of Examples By default, the full ERQA benchmark consists of 400 examples. python eval_harness.py --num_examples 10 Complete Examples Example with custom arguments for Gemini: python eval_harness.py --api gemini --model gemini-2.0-pro --gemini_api_key YOUR_API_KEY Example with custom arguments for OpenAI: python eval_harness.py --api openai --model gpt-4o-mini --openai_api_key YOUR_API_KEY Example with multiple API keys and a keys file: python eval_harness.py --api_keys_file ./gemini_keys.txt Command-line Arguments --tfrecord_path : Path to the TFRecord file (default: './data/erqa.tfrecord') --api : API to use: 'gemini' or 'openai' (default: 'gemini') --model : Model name to use (defaults: 'gemini-2.0-flash-exp' for Gemini, 'gpt-4o' for OpenAI) Available Gemini models include: gemini-2.0-flash-exp, gemini-2.0-pro, gemini-2.0-pro-exp-02-05 --gemini_api_key : Gemini API key (can be specified multiple times for multiple keys) --openai_api_key : OpenAI API key (can be specified multiple times for multiple keys) --api_keys_file : Path to a file containing API keys (one per line, format: "gemini:KEY" or "openai:KEY") --num_examples : Number of examples to process (default: 1) --max_retries : Maximum number of retries per API key on resource exhaustion (default: 2) --max_tokens : Maximum number of tokens in the response (for OpenAI only, default: 300) --connection_retries : Maximum number of retries for connection errors (for column5: Apptronik - Home Join Us Get Started Robots for Humans Watch The Video Intelligent, Mobile, Dexterous Apollo is designed to bring AI into the physical world. With advanced mobility, dexterous manipulation, and the ability to learn new skills, Apollo can help take on physically demanding work in environments built for people. As industries face growing labor challenges, humanoid robots offer a new way forward: adaptable machines that can support human teams, increase productivity, and help keep essential work moving. Form That Fits the Work Apollo’s modular design gives teams flexibility in how robots are deployed. With both bipedal and wheeled mobility options, Apollo can adapt to different environments, workflows, and operational needs. Whether navigating human-centered spaces or moving efficiently through structured facilities, Apollo is designed to meet the work where it happens. Human-Centered by Design Apollo was created with a simple purpose: to help people. By supporting human teams with physically demanding, repetitive, or potentially hazardous work, Apollo can help reduce strain, improve safety, and give people more time to focus on higher-value tasks. That same human-first approach extends to how Apollo communicates. Thoughtful visual cues, voice interaction, and at-a-glance status displays help people understand what Apollo is doing, what it needs, and how to work alongside it with greater confidence. Built for the Real World Apollo is more than a robot - it’s a platform for scalable humanoid deployment. Apptronik brings together advanced hardware, embodied AI, and fleet-level tools to support robots that can be managed, improved, and deployed across real operations.The result is a complete approach to humanoid robotics: one designed not just to demonstrate what’s possible, but to make useful robots part of everyday work. Apollo for Manufacturing Support production teams with flexible automation for material handling, line-side tasks, inspection, and repetitive workflows all without redesigning the factory floor. Learn More Apollo for Warehouse Improve fulfillment and logistics operations with a humanoid robot designed to help pick, pack, move goods, and reduce the physical strain of repetitive work. Learn More Apollo for Retail Help retail teams manage inventory, replenishment, and back-of-house tasks so employees can spend more time focused on customers. Learn More One Platform for the Future of Work The future of robotics won’t be defined by a single form factor or a single use case. It will be defined by adaptable platforms that can learn, evolve, and meet people wherever support is needed. Apollo brings that future closer. Today, it is built to take on meaningful work in industries like manufacturing, warehousing, and logistics. Over time, the same foundation of mobility, manipulation, intelligence, and human-centered interaction can extend into more complex environments, from hospitals and retail spaces to eldercare and ultimately, the home. One Robot, Endless Possibilities Apollo's adaptability ensures it can meet various needs, from industrial applications to potential household uses. This approach not only addresses current labor market gaps but also anticipates future needs, providing a scalable solution that can grow and evolve with technological advancements & market demands. column5: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics - Google Developers Blog Search Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics OCT. 13, 2026 Kanishka Rao Principal Software Engineer Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Mail Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI. You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark , which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model. As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas: Robot control → Mobile manipulation with MuJoCo practice, zero-shot robot control, and closed-loop steering of video world models. Real2Sim → Reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from robot camera feeds, egocentric human video, or hand-drawn paper sketches. Physical understanding → Agentic multimodal hindsight labeling including detailed understanding of dexterity, dense value functions and progress estimation. Research and self-improvement → Action improvement via simulation and iterative self-improvement on hardware. Unlocking robot control with Argon 1. Spot mobile manipulation: Putting in the trash bin with MuJoCo practice Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Spot Mobile Manipulation — Real-to-Sim-to-Real foot-pedal trash bin disposal: Spot picking up the soda can, checking its wrist camera, practicing 3-leg tripod balance in MuJoCo, stepping on the foot pedal, verifying hand centering in the open bin, and dropping the can inside. Prompt: There's a Diet Coke can behind you and another on the black table on your left. Use the spot-mobile-manipulation skill to pick them up and trash them in the black foot-pedal bin. Before stepping down on the pedal, verify in the front cameras that your front-right foot target is centered on the pedal, and use a 2-agent verification swarm (foot-verifier and hand-verifier) to verify both the foot-pedal step and the 3D hand-in-bin alignment before releasing. Plain text Copied 2. Zero-shot control Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Left: 3rd-person real robot view; Right: calibrated wrist camera with projected 2 cm world coordinates and jaw-closing reticle. Prompt: [Attached: wrist_cam.png, obs.json] Task: Get the robot arm to reorient the mug upright and put the napkin inside the mug. ## Execution Discipline - Simply output 1 sentence observation followed immediately by your `curl` command (with `# Plan:` on Turn 1 and `# Thought:` on every turn). Everything needed is in `obs.json` and the calibrated reticle/grid drawn on `wrist_cam.png`. ## Visual Coordinate Reference (Annotated on wrist_cam.png) - `+X` (UP in image): Away from robot base | `-X` (DOWN): Towards robot base - `+Y` (LEFT in image): World left | `-Y` (RIGHT): World right - `+Z`: Height above table | `Yellow numbers`: World (X, Y) in centimetres (2 cm grid at `grid_z`) - `Cyan + crosshair`: Current 3D pinch center - `Cyan [ + ] brackets`: Current jaw opening and closing line - `Green line`: Current object long-axis orientation (`yaw_deg`: 0° = vertical along +X, 90° = horizontal along +Y) - `pitch_deg = 90°`: Straight down (-Z) top-down grasp/place; `pitch_deg < 60°`: Tilted coaxial approach along finger axis ## Closed-Loop Turn Workflow 1. Inspect current state & view `wrist_cam.png`: `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/obs` (returns `ee_pos`, `holding`, `status`, `workspace`, `wrist_cam_path`). 2. Select VLM call granularity upfront on Turn 1: - Coarse (2–4 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> `place` -> `done` - Pre-Grasp Hover Verify (4–7 calls): `look_at` -> `goto(z=0.04)` (verify cyan `[ + ]` brackets straddle target) -> `grasp` -> `place_until_contact` -> `done` - Fine Visual Servoing (8–20 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> pre-pose `goto` -> closed-loop `move_by` / `move_until_contact` -> `done` 3. Send motion primitives (`POST /plan`) and verify visually after every turn in the updated `wrist_cam.png`. If `status == "grasp_failed"`, call `robot.look_at(...)` to re-observe and recover closed-loop. ## Code-as-Policies Primitives (`POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/plan`) robot.look_at(x=0.35, y=0.13, z=0.14, grid_z=0.015) x, y = robot.deproject(u=0.52, v=0.48, z_plane=0.015) robot.grasp(x=x, y=y, z=0.015, yaw_deg=-35, pitch_deg=90) robot.place(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.075) robot.place_until_contact(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.015, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002) robot.goto(x=0.28, y=0.05, z=0.04, arc_z=0.14, pitch_deg=25, azimuth_deg=90, roll_deg=0, speed=0.10) robot.move_by(forward=0.025, dz=-0.002, dpitch_deg=-3, droll_deg=5, speed=0.04) robot.move_until_contact(dz=-0.06, speed=0.03, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002) robot.open_gripper() / robot.close_gripper() / robot.home() / robot.done() Plain text Copied 3. Omni control Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles ( G, R, A, N, O ) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N . Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Iterative Video World Model Steering Dexterous Hands: 33-Step Steered Video Rollout Spelling A-R-G-O-N. Prompt: Goal: {task_goal} You are steering a video world model (Gemini Omni) in an iterative visual feedback loop. Inspect the attached frames from the latest rollout and write the next timestamped action prompt for the video world model: - Break complex motions into one simple, single-direction action at a time. - Keep inactive hands retracted and avoid blocking the camera's view of objects in the workspace. - Explicitly state which areas of the workspace become empty after an object moves. - Use [MM:SS.mmm] timestamps for each action beat and wrap your output in <omni_prompt> tags. Example format (sample timestamps only, not the full prompt): <omni_prompt> [00:00.000] Character A's left hand rests at the side while the right hand reaches toward the target object. [00:02.500] Character A's right fingertips push the object smoothly into the center of the table, leaving its starting area empty. [00:05.000] Character A's right hand opens and retracts to the side so all placed objects remain in clear view of the camera. </omni_prompt> Plain text Copied Unlocking Real2Sim with Argon 1. Robot view to simulation Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Left (Real View): synchronized real robot camera feeds; Right (Simulated): 3D MuJoCo scene reconstructed and calibrated by Argon. Prompt: [Attached: robot_rollout_episode] Build a MuJoCo scene of the robot and reconstructed task objects. When each episode is replayed frame by frame, by driving the robot joints toward the logged observation.state with joint-space PD. Iterate using two verification objectives: (1) Visual match: MuJoCo renders from the head_left, left_wrist, and right_wrist cameras line up with, and look like, those real observations. (2) Physical match: the simulated contact force/torque on each Sharpa fingertip, in the sensor frame, matches the logged tactile_force in timing, magnitude and direction. What you can tune happens before simulation starts: (1) Static object assets: realistic geometry, collision shapes, mass, inertia, friction and joints, with appearance close to the real objects, plus the initial object poses at t = 0. (2) Offline-planned robot commands, changed only in frames where the real fingertips are near an object. Each command must stay within 0.55 rad (arm joints) and 0.65 rad (hand joints) of the logged teleop trajectory. Everywhere else, replay the logged trajectory unchanged. No sim cheating: task objects may move only through real MuJoCo contact with the robot hands and the environment (mj_step). Not allowed after t = 0: changing MjModel parameters; applying external forces or torques to objects; welds or equality constraints; feedforward torques beyond joint-space PD; setting or rolling back object qpos/qvel; disabling or excluding collisions; reporting contact forces that don't come from the MuJoCo solver (for example, copying the logged tactile readings). Immediately present the reconstructed scene and rollout results as an interactive HTML session viewer with one page per episode, showing: - At the bottom: A synced timeline (play, scrub, speed control) that drives every panel. - On the left panel: An interactive 3D Blender scene showing the simulated robot and objects, showing contact points and force arrows as replay progresses. - On the right panel: Real vs. sim camera views side by side for all 3 cameras. Real vs. sim finger force visualizations. Plain text Copied 2. Human view to simulation Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Human View to Simulation — Egocentric Human Video to Dexterous Humanoid Twin: Left shows the input egocentric human RGB video; Right shows the synchronized 500 Hz MuJoCo + Blender Cycles multi-view simulation rollout. Prompt: [Attached: egocentric_human_video.mp4, candidate_sim_views.png, hand_3d_keypoints.json] You are building a physically solvable 500 Hz MuJoCo manipulation environment (`scene.xml`) and studio Blender render that faithfully reproduces the tabletop task shown in `egocentric_human_video.mp4` on a bimanual humanoid robot with 22-DoF dexterous five-fingered hands: 1. Scene Reconstruction & Camera Calibration: - Identify only the manipulation-relevant objects (the grasped target object and the receiving container or landmark) and triangulate their 3D tabletop coordinates from the egocentric camera intrinsics/extrinsics. - Replace crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed 3D meshes so concave containers (nested bowls, recessed wooden trays, open bins) support physical interior placement. 2. 500 Hz Dexterous Motion-Fitting Stress Test: - Retarget the 3D human wrist and finger keypoints to the humanoid's 7-DoF arm and 22-DoF hand joints, and step the trajectory in MuJoCo at 500 Hz (dt = 0.002s) with zero kinematic weld constraints. - Verify opposing thumb-and-finger force closure, clean object lift (> 2 cm), and stable final placement inside or beside the target landmark. Plain text Copied 3. Sketch to simulation With Argon, a developer can snap a photo of a rough pen-and-paper sketch—showing an Apollo 2 humanoid throwing a ball along a parabolic arc to topple a 3-2-1 stack of boxes on a table—and have Argon automatically construct the GPU-accelerated mujoco_warp scene, synthesize a balanced 76-DoF whole-body and five-finger throw trajectory, verify 6/6 target knockdown in closed-loop physics, and export a Blender 4.5 Cycles render. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Sketch to Simulation — Hand-Drawn Sketch to Dexterous Humanoid Trajectory & Cycles Render. Prompt: [Attached: hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg] Translate this hand-drawn sketch into a physically verified humanoid simulation in `mujoco_warp` and a raytraced Blender Cycles video: 1. Scene & Kinematic Setup from Sketch: - Parse the spatial layout from `hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg`: place the 76-DoF humanoid (32-DoF body equipped with two 22-DoF five-finger dexterous hands) at the origin facing a table holding a 3-2-1 pyramid of 6 rigid target boxes, with a projectile sphere grasped in the right five-finger hand. 2. Whole-Body Balance & Dexterous Throw Synthesis: - Synthesize a 50 Hz whole-body throwing trajectory (140 steps, 2.80 s) across four phases: (1) stable stance & 5-finger power grasp closure, (2) torso/shoulder wind-up with ankle-hip Center-of-Mass compensation, (3) forward whipping acceleration, and (4) synchronized 22-DoF five-finger opening at peak hand velocity so the ball launches on a ballistic arc into the pyramid's second-tier center of mass. - Verify in `mujoco_warp` contact physics that the humanoid maintains upright balance (< 3 cm pelvis drift) and knocks down all 6 target boxes. Plain text Copied Unlocking physical understanding with Argon 1. Hindsight labeling and data quality Argon has precise physical understanding of dexterous manipulation and can provide detailed segmentation and text labeling from video. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Argon Multi-Granularity Hindsight & Telemetry HUD. Prompt: [Attached: Aloha2_Origami_20250309.mp4] Produce a time-aligned multi-granularity hindsight annotation JSON with four levels: 1. G1_episode_instruction: Concise imperative sentence describing the overall manipulation goal. 2. G2_subtasks: Contiguous semantic subtask phases specifying which arm(s) anchor vs. fold/rotate the object. 3. G3_atomic_primitives: Fine-grained contact-level primitives (3–15s) aligned with grasp closure, crease sweeps, release, or retry attempts. 4. quality_control_and_reweighting: Hold task_progress_pct flat during non-progressing slip/delamination retry loops and downweight them (0.15x–0.25x) for Behavior Cloning. Plain text Copied 2. Find the odd ball To recreate the classic 12-ball balance scale puzzle with robots, Argon builds a bimanual Franka FR3 MuJoCo environment with 12 visually identical pool balls (one secretly heavier or lighter) and an articulated Roberval two-pan balance scale. It then writes a vision-only closed-loop solver that triangulates the balls from stereo RGB cameras, visually reads the scale tilt after each weighing, and isolates the odd ball into the Heavy (Red) or Light (Blue) tray within 3 weighings. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Find the Odd Ball (Vision-Only Closed-Loop Solver): Dual-arm Franka FR3 weighing candidate balls on the Gold/Teal pans, reading stereo scale tilt , and isolating the confirmed Heavy odd ball into the Red tray in 3 weighings. Prompt: # Prompt 1 — Physics-Accurate MuJoCo Environment & Benchmark Generation Make a MuJoCo environment where a dual-arm robot (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers on a shared tabletop) is tasked to solve the classic 12-ball balance scale weight puzzle from https://www.mathsisfun.com/pool_balls_solution.html. 1. Create 12 visually indistinguishable pool balls in a 2x6 starting rack (11 standard 150 g, 1 odd ball either 270 g or 30 g). 2. Build a functional two-pan Roberval balance scale at the center of the table with parallelogram equality constraints (`mjEQ_JOINT`) so the Left (Gold) and Right (Teal) pans stay horizontal, plus Red (Heavy) and Blue (Light) submission trays. 3. Track distinct settled weighings (`weighing_count`) and reward `1.00` for isolating the true odd ball in the correct Heavy/Light tray within <= 3 weighings. # Prompt 2 — Closed-Loop Vision-Only Solver Implement an independent closed-loop policy relying strictly on stereo RGB camera inputs (`head_camera_left_rgb_image`, `head_camera_right_rgb_image`) and robot proprioception (`add_privileged_task_observations=False`): 1. Segment the 12 balls, Gold/Teal pans, and Red/Blue trays in both stereo views and triangulate their 3D coordinates. 2. Visually read the balance scale tilt after each weighing from stereo vertical pixel disparity (+1 = left heavier, -1 = right heavier, 0 = balanced). 3. Rotate the gripper wrist yaw by 90 degrees when grasping/placing inside the narrow scale pans to clear the raised rims, and isolate the odd ball into the Red or Blue tray within <= 3 weighings. Plain text Copied 3. Value function Argon is a general value function for robotics tasks. Evaluated on a 60-second bimanual ring-sorting episode from a human UMI dataset, Argon iteratively inspects synchronized head, left-gripper, and right-gripper camera feeds around contact transitions to generate dense value function / task progress predictions and decompose the trajectory into 28 segments with positive, neutral, and negative progress slopes. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Value Function: Synchronized 3-camera UMI playback (head, left gripper, right gripper) locked to animated task progress curve and bimanual segment annotations. Prompt: [Attached: umi_head.mp4, umi_left_gripper.mp4, umi_right_gripper.mp4] Look at 3 videos of human wearing a gripper performing activities from head, left, right gripper views. Look at the videos thoroughly and give a detailed plot of progress at the task (with positive, neutral, negative slope), identifying important segments in the video and labeling the activities. Look at individual frames or subsegments of the video if necessary to get a better understanding. Plain text Copied Unlocking research and self-improvement with Argon 1. Action improvement via simulation Argon can generate new data in simulation to improve performance of generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models. Starting from a single RGB photo of the real tabletop, Argon autonomously builds a calibrated MuJoCo simulation twin, defines new tasks, and synthesizes a closed-loop motion generator to collect 4,500+ domain-randomized episodes in simulation—boosting real-world physical robot Success Rate from 56% to 75% and reducing completion time from 35s to 24s . Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Action Improvement via Simulation: improves the real-world evaluation benchmark (56% → 75% Success Rate and 35s → 24s Completion Time). Prompt: [Attached: real_tabletop_photo.jpg] You are given a single overhead RGB camera photo (`real_tabletop_photo.jpg`) of a bimanual robot workspace (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers and 4 RGB cameras) facing a table arranged with photobooth party props. 1. Reconstruct procedural 3D meshes and compound MuJoCo collision primitives for all 9 party props matching their real-world dimensions, colors, and resting poses, including spring-hinged deformable crown panels for the soft plush cap. 2. Define a 77-task single-arm and bimanual curriculum (pick-and-place, uprighting, directional pushing, mid-air handovers, bimanual scoop-and-push, and pipelined table clearing). 3. Synthesize a closed-loop IK trajectory generator across ±10 cm pose randomization, verify `reward == 1.0` in MuJoCo physics, and export 4,500+ episodes for VLA fine-tuning. Plain text Copied 2. Self-Improvement for visual pick and place On a simple 6-DoF arm, Argon iteratively self-improves both execution speed and placement accuracy on a pick and place task via trial and self-reflection. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video SO-101 Vision-Guided Pick-and-Place — Iterative Hardware Self-Improvement Across Iterations 1 → 2 → 3: Iteration 1 (58.9s), Iteration 2 (22.9s, grazed box rim on drop), and Iteration 3 (17.4s, dead-center drop). Prompt: # Stage 1 — Measure Objects & Dry-Run Plan (No Hardware Motion) Stage 1: measure objects — find the objects and plan the whole motion. The arm does not move in this stage. A. I put a LEGO brick and a box on the table in front of the arm, and the wooden box to one side. Find the brick and the wooden box in the image. And also in the real world. Show this in an annotated image. B. A dry-run plan (no hardware). Write the planner to pick and place the lego block. Print the plan table, draw all poses onto the overhead image, and stop. Do not move the robot. Report with evidence. # Stage 2 — Pre-Pick Hover & Wrist-Camera Verification Stage 2: Put the gripper above the brick without touching it, and verify with the wrist camera that the arm and the vision agree. Please record executions with both cameras (compressed video is OK). # Stage 3 (Autonomous Pick-and-Place → Self-Improvement → Optimization): 1. Execute autonomously: Turn the Stage 1 dry run into a real grasp, lift, and place into the wooden box. Run it yourself subject to safety rules from AGENTS.md. 2. Self-improve: When an attempt fails, diagnose it yourself. Review your own logs and wrist/overhead footage, find the root cause, check the fix in a dry run, and retry. 3. Optimize on feedback: Once it succeeds, make it at least 2× faster within safety limits (rule R5) unless I authorize more, or give feedback. Plain text Copied 3. One-prompt robotics paper reproductions in MuJoCo WebAssembly With a single prompt per paper, Argon reads a robotics control manuscript and any released checkpoints, ports the physics model and closed-loop controller (from 7-network hierarchical locomotion in DeepLoco and 50 Hz PPO actors in HUSKY to Web Worker iLQR in Whole-Body MPC ) into self-contained MuJoCo WebAssembly browser labs, and verifies them in headless Chromium. Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video Five Landmark Legged & Humanoid Papers Running Live in Browser (MuJoCo WASM): Robotic Soccer OP3 1v1, DeepLoco, Massively Parallel Deep RL ANYmal C, Whole-Body MPC Go2, and HUSKY G1 Skateboarding (from 68 interactive browser sandboxes reproduced by Argon). Prompt: [Attached: paper.pdf, optional author_checkpoints/ or urdf_assets/] Reproduce the paper "<Paper Title & arXiv ID>" from scratch in MuJoCo WebAssembly and deploy a self-contained browser lab + visual essay: 1. Match the paper's exact physics timestep, actuator gains (kp/kv), torque limits, and kinematic constraints in MuJoCo XML, and run real neural inference or Web Worker iLQR in JavaScript at the paper's exact control rates. 2. Build `index.html` (Spatial UI simulator with camera presets, live telemetry plots, and disturbance injection) and `scrollytelling.html` (interactive visual essay). 3. Run a headless Chromium (Playwright) verification loop asserting 0 console errors and non-zero task progress over 300+ frames. Plain text Copied Advancing embodied intelligence with Argon Argon bridges coding, visual perception, physics simulation, and embodied robot control. By reasoning natively over multi-view video, 3D geometry, contact mechanics, and proprioceptive telemetry, Argon understands not just what objects are in a scene, but how they physically interact with agents to accomplish whole-body dexterous tasks. Gemini 4 Argon marks an important milestone accelerating the path toward physical AGI. By building this core intelligence, our goal is to enable robotics that can work alongside humans to solve complex challenges. Getting started You can start building with Gemini 4 Argon today across Google’s developer platforms: Google AI Studio : Available to Google AI Ultra subscribers. Gemini 4 Argon is Google's frontier model that excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It's the first model in the Gemini 4 family. This document covers what's new with 4 Argon, the API conventions it enforces, how to migrate to it, and a quickstart. For an overview of the Gemini 4 family, see Get started with Gemini 4 . What's new in Gemini 4 Argon? Unified input and output token limit : 4 Argon has a unified 1,048,576-token limit that includes both input and output tokens (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response). Long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens : Extends generation beyond the single-request output limit (65,536 tokens, or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming direct HTTP requests) up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus your input tokens) on GenerateContent . The Google Gen AI SDK handles continuation_token automatically across requests, or you can manage continuation_token in your own continuation loop. Thinking levels : LOW , MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon ), and HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive ). Implicit caching with durable caching : Implicit caching applies automatically to shared prompt prefixes of 6,144 tokens or more, with durable caching enabled by default. Explicit context caching isn't supported. Agentic video understanding : Generally available, and off by default. Quickstart Before you begin, you must authenticate to Agent Platform using Application Default Credentials (ADC) or an API key. See Get started with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform for more information. In the following code blocks, replace PROJECT_ID with your project ID. Try it in Agent Studio To test prompts and configure gemini-4-argon in the Agent Studio UI: Open Agent Studio in your Google Cloud project and select gemini-4-argon under the Gemini group. In Model settings , configure: Thinking level : Choose Low , Medium (default), or High . Region : Select Global , us , or eu . Output token limit : Set between 32,768 and 1,048,576 ( 1,048,576 default). Agent Studio handles continuation tokens automatically for responses over the single-request limit. Installation Upgrade to the latest Google Gen AI SDK ( google-genai >= 2.30.1 for Python, @google/genai >= 2.29.1 for JavaScript, >= 1.74.0 for Go, >= 1.77.0 for Java, >= 1.26.0 for .NET, or >= 1.6.0 for Kotlin): pip install --upgrade "google-genai>=2.30.1" Basic request Python (GenerateContent) from google import genai from google.genai import types client = genai . Client ( enterprise = True , project = " PROJECT_ID " , location = "global" ) response = client . models . generate_content ( model = "gemini-4-argon" , contents = "Design a lock-free ring buffer in Rust for multi-producer, single-consumer telemetry ingestion." , config = types . GenerateContentConfig ( thinking_config = types . ThinkingConfig ( thinking_level = "MEDIUM" , # Default: "MEDIUM" (Valid: "LOW", "MEDIUM", "HIGH") ), ), ) print ( response . text ) Python (Interactions API) from google import genai client = genai . Client ( enterprise = True , project = " PROJECT_ID " , location = "global" ) # Turn 1: Initial request (stored server-side by default) turn1 = client . interactions . create ( model = "gemini-4-argon" , input = "Design a lock-free ring buffer in Rust for multi-producer, single-consumer telemetry ingestion." , store = True , ) print ( turn1 . output_text ) # Turn 2: Continue the conversation using previous_interaction_id turn2 = client . interactions . create ( model = "gemini-4-argon" , input = "Add a bounded backpressure policy and unit tests for concurrent writers." , previous_interaction_id = turn1 . id , ) print ( turn2 . output_text ) REST curl -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $( gcloud auth application-default print-access-token ) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/ PROJECT_ID /locations/global/publishers/google/models/gemini-4-argon:generateContent" \ -d '{ "contents": [ { "role": "user", "parts": [ { "text": "Provide an architectural review of this Go interface." } ] } ], "generationConfig": { "thinkingConfig": { "thinkingLevel": "MEDIUM" } } }' Structured output from pydantic import BaseModel , Field from google import genai from google.genai import types class ArchitectureReview ( BaseModel ): component : str = Field ( description = "Service or module name" ) bottlenecks : list [ str ] = Field ( description = "Throughput or latency bottlenecks" ) recommended_changes : list [ str ] = Field ( description = "Concrete refactoring steps" ) client = genai . Client ( enterprise = True , project = " PROJECT_ID " , location = "global" ) response = client . models . generate_content ( model = "gemini-4-argon" , contents = "Review a synchronous order-processing pipeline backed by a single primary database at 15,000 writes/sec." , config = types . GenerateContentConfig ( response_mime_type = "application/json" , response_schema = ArchitectureReview , thinking_config = types . ThinkingConfig ( thinking_level = "HIGH" ), ), ) print ( response . text ) Long decodes By default, a single API request generates up to 65,536 output tokens (or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming direct HTTP requests), where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response. To generate completions up to 1,048,576 tokens on GenerateContent ( v1beta1 ), set max_output_tokens greater than 65,536 for streaming requests or greater than 32,768 for non-streaming requests (up to 1,048,576). The Google Gen AI SDK automatically follows continuation_token across requests when finish_reason is CONTINUATION (set automatic_continuation=False in GenerateContentConfig to disable automatic continuation), or you can pass continuation_token in a custom loop. Note: Known issue : Long decoding on GenerateContent ( generateContent and streamGenerateContent ) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1 ). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless you override http_options={'api_version': 'v1'} ; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path as shown in the following example. Python (SDK - Recommended) from google import genai from google.genai import types client = genai . Client ( enterprise = True , project = " PROJECT_ID " , location = "global" ) # Automatic continuation is enabled by default in google-genai >= 2.30.1. # Chunks across all continuation requests are yielded as a single stream. for chunk in client . models . generate_content_stream ( model = "gemini-4-argon" , contents = "Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem." , config = types . GenerateContentConfig ( max_output_tokens = 256000 , thinking_config = types . ThinkingConfig ( thinking_level = "HIGH" ), ), ): print ( chunk . text , end = "" ) # Set automatic_continuation=False to disable automatic continuation. for chunk in client . models . generate_content_stream ( model = "gemini-4-argon" , contents = "Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem." , config = types . GenerateContentConfig ( thinking_config = types . ThinkingConfig ( thinking_level = "HIGH" ), automatic_continuation = False , ), ): print ( chunk . text , end = "" ) REST (Custom continuation loop) # Request 1: Initial request with maxOutputTokens > 32,768 curl -s -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $( gcloud auth application-default print-access-token ) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/ PROJECT_ID /locations/global/publishers/google/models/gemini-4-argon:generateContent" \ -d '{ "contents": [{ "role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem."}] }], "generationConfig": { "maxOutputTokens": 131072, "thinkingConfig": {"thinkingLevel": "HIGH"} } }' # Request 2: Resend the original request with top-level continuationToken # from Request 1 (candidates[0].continuationToken) curl -s -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $( gcloud auth application-default print-access-token ) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/projects/ PROJECT_ID /locations/global/publishers/google/models/gemini-4-argon:generateContent" \ -d '{ "contents": [{ "role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "Write a complete formal proof of the prime number theorem."}] }], "continuationToken": "CONTINUATION_TOKEN_FROM_REQUEST_1", "generationConfig": { "maxOutputTokens": 131072, "thinkingConfig": {"thinkingLevel": "HIGH"} } }' Mandatory API rules and behavioral conventions Important: Setting thinking_budget or thinking_level="MINIMAL" returns an HTTP 400 error. Valid values for thinking_level are LOW , MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon ), and HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive ). Gemini 4 Argon enforces the following conventions: Thinking levels : 4 Argon supports three thinking_level values ( thinking_budget and MINIMAL return an HTTP 400 validation error): Thinking level Recommended workloads HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive ) Multi-file software engineering, formal proofs, architecture design, and vulnerability discovery. MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon ) General coding, tool use, document Q&A, and video understanding. LOW Classification, summarization, and metadata extraction. Unified input and output token limit and single-request output limits : 1,048,576 is the overall token limit of the model and includes both input and output tokens (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response). max_output_tokens controls the output token cap for the generation (up to 1,048,576 minus your input tokens); setting max_output_tokens greater than 1,048,576 returns an HTTP 400 error. To avoid unintended long completions, the default single-request output limit (thinking + model response) is 65,536 tokens (or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming direct HTTP requests). Long decodes : How long decode works : Long decode splits a generation up to 1,048,576 tokens across multiple GenerateContent inferences. For example, if a task requires 256,000 output tokens (including thoughts, function calls, and the final response), the first streaming request generates up to 65,536 output tokens and emits finish_reason=CONTINUATION with an encrypted continuation_token containing a hash of the original prompt and the generation state up to that point. Including continuation_token in subsequent requests with the original prompt continues generation from where it left off until continuation_token is no longer emitted and finish_reason=STOP . (In Agent Studio, setting the output token limit greater than 65,536 up to 1,048,576 handles continuation tokens automatically.) When to use long decode : Most requests finish within the per-request limit (65,536 tokens, or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming REST calls). Use long decode only when one response needs more output than that. Long decode gives the model more room to reason; it does not make answers longer (use thinking_level to control reasoning depth). Workload Use long decode? Why Hard math, science, research, and formal proofs Yes The model can spend more than 65,536 tokens to explore and check its reasoning. The hardest coding and agentic tasks Yes Some tasks need more than 65,536 tokens of thinking and code in one response. Most coding and agentic tasks finish under 65,536 tokens. Evaluation harnesses that stop at the output limit Yes Long decode prevents cut-off answers when the model spends an entire 65,536- or 32,768-token request on thinking. Chat, Q&A, summarization, classification, and extraction No These tasks finish well under 32,768 tokens. Requests for a fixed length, such as "write a 700,000-word book" No The model does not follow length targets. Agents that call tools in many short turns No Each turn is short. Large outputs on each turn fill the unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit quickly. Prompts near the 1,048,576-token input limit No Output can use only 1,048,576 tokens minus your input. Latency-sensitive requests No Long decode can run for several minutes. Choosing a continuation option : Choose one of two options. Most developers use Option 1. All options reach the same 1,048,576-token limit on gemini-4-argon and gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive . Dimension Option 1: Google Gen AI SDK (recommended) Option 2: Your own streaming loop ( streamGenerateContent ) Option 2: Your own non-streaming loop ( generateContent ) Who starts each segment Google Gen AI SDKs: Python ( google-genai ) 2.30.1, JavaScript ( @google/genai ) 2.29.1, Go 1.74.0, Java 1.77.0, .NET 1.26.0, and Kotlin 1.6.0. You set max_output_tokens . Your code, at each checkpoint or after a dropped stream Your code, every 32,768 tokens Tokens per request Up to 65,536 per segment 65,536 per stream, with a checkpoint every 5,000 tokens after 32,768 32,768 per request Time limit per request 20 minutes 20 minutes 20 minutes Storage No server storage (ZDR-compliant) No server storage (ZDR-compliant) No server storage (ZDR-compliant) Best for Most applications REST callers and custom harnesses that stream Simple evaluation harnesses Implementation rules and limitations : v1beta1 API requirement (known issue) : Long decoding ( continuation_token ) on GenerateContent ( generateContent and streamGenerateContent ) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1 ). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is specified in http_options ; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path. Long decode isn't supported on the Interactions API. SDK versions and OpenAI compatibility : Upgrade to the latest Google Gen AI SDK ( google-genai >= 2.30.1 for Python, @google/genai >= 2.29.1 for JavaScript, >= 1.74.0 for Go, >= 1.77.0 for Java, >= 1.26.0 for .NET, or >= 1.6.0 for Kotlin). Older SDK versions and the OpenAI compatibility layer cannot retrieve long completions using continuation tokens. For custom client implementations, refer to the Google Gen AI SDK reference implementations in Python and JavaScript/TypeScript . Resend the original request with continuation_token : In a custom loop, set max_output_tokens greater than 65,536 (streaming) or 32,768 (unary) up to 1,048,576, and resend the original contents , system_instruction , and tools on every continuation request along with the latest continuation_token (a top-level field on GenerateContentRequest in REST, or in GenerateContentConfig in the Google Gen AI SDK). Don't append partial model output into contents or send a follow-up prompt asking the model to continue. Continue through thinking-only requests : Loop while finish_reason is CONTINUATION and continuation_token is present, even if a request spent all 32,768 or 65,536 tokens thinking ( parts: [{"text": ""}] ). If finish_reason is MAX_TOKENS when continuation_token is present, generation reached the requested max_output_tokens cap—raise max_output_tokens in the request. Combine accumulated parts into a single model turn for multi-turn history only after STOP . Token counting, compaction, and 95% implicit cache discount : In the Python Google Gen AI SDK ( generate_content and generate_content_stream ), the final response or chunk's usage_metadata accumulates total billed tokens across continuation requests. Because each continuation request re-prefills prior partial completions as input tokens, prompt_token_count increases cumulatively across continuation requests—don't use prompt_token_count to trigger context compaction in agent harnesses. Instead, read initial_prompt_token_count (on GenerateContentResponse or usage_metadata ), and wait until GenerateContent completes (no continuation_token present) before compacting. In custom REST loops, usage_metadata is cumulative within each request; sum the final prompt_token_count , cached_content_token_count , candidates_token_count , and thoughts_token_count across requests. Each continuation request re-prefills the prompt plus prior decoded tokens and automatically receives the 95% implicit context caching discount (6,144-token minimum) when requests run back-to-back within the 15–20 minute cache TTL. streamGenerateContent and generateContent return usage_metadata at the end of each request (65,536 streaming / 32,768 unary), and billing occurs at the end of the request. Ignored sampling parameters ( temperature , top_k , top_p ) : The backend ignores custom values. Control reasoning depth with thinking_level , and output format with response_schema . Unsupported parameters ( frequency_penalty , presence_penalty , candidate_count ) : These return an HTTP 400 error. Remove them from your requests. Context caching : Explicit context caching isn't supported. Implicit caching (with durable caching enabled by default) applies automatically to shared prompt prefixes of 6,144 tokens or more, so put static content at the start of your prompt. Agentic video : Uploaded videos default to media_processing="static" . Set media_processing="agentic" to enable agentic video processing . Token counting and billing : Every token the model processes is counted and billed, including thinking tokens and internal tool system instructions and function declarations when using grounding. Grounding with Google Search also remains billed per query. Function calling : Turn symmetry : Each FunctionResponse must match the id , name , and order of the preceding FunctionCall . Sequential execution : Prefer sequential tool execution turns in multi-step tool loops. Pre-tool formatting : Separate inline instructions with \n\n and avoid unstructured text before tool calls. To log intermediate state before a tool call, use a dedicated function declaration: { "name" : "update" , "description" : "Update working notes before tool execution" , "parameters" : { "type" : "OBJECT" , "properties" : { "previous_step" : { "type" : "STRING" }, "plan" : { "type" : "STRING" }, "next_step" : { "type" : "STRING" } }, "required" : [ "previous_step" , "plan" , "next_step" ] } } Chat sequence validation : History payloads can't end with a model role turn. Prefilled model turns aren't supported. Migrate to 4 Argon from 3.1 Pro The following behavior is different from gemini-3.1-pro-preview : 4 Argon has a unified 1,048,576-token limit across input and output (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response), instead of separate input and output limits. Single-request output is capped at 65,536 tokens (or 32,768 tokens for non-streaming direct HTTP requests), and can be extended up to 1,048,576 tokens using long decodes on GenerateContent (handled automatically in the Google Gen AI SDK, or using continuation_token in custom loops). thinking_budget returns an HTTP 400 error instead of being mapped to a thinking level. MINIMAL also returns an error. Explicit context caching isn't supported. Every token the model processes is billed, including internal tool system instructions and function declarations when using grounding. For a side-by-side comparison, see Migrate from Gemini 3.1 Pro . client = genai.Client( enterprise=True, project="PROJECT_ID", location="global", # Supports "global", "us", and "eu" ) response = client.models.generate_content( - model="gemini-3.1-pro-preview", + model="gemini-4-argon", contents=prompt, config=types.GenerateContentConfig( - temperature=0.0, - cached_content="projects/.../cachedContents/...", # Explicit caching unsupported thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig( - thinking_budget=16384, # Returns HTTP 400 instead of mapping silently - thinking_level="MINIMAL", # MINIMAL unsupported on Gemini 4 Argon + thinking_level="MEDIUM", # Valid: "LOW", "MEDIUM" (default), "HIGH" ), ), ) To migrate from gemini-3.1-pro-preview , do the following: Update the model ID to gemini-4-argon (or gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive for Fairwind-approved cybersecurity workloads). Upgrade to the latest Google Gen AI SDK and account for the unified input and output token limit : Upgrade to google-genai >= 2.30.1 (Python), @google/genai >= 2.29.1 (JavaScript), or the equivalent latest Google Gen AI SDK. Input and output tokens (including thinking and function calls) share the unified 1,048,576-token limit. For outputs exceeding 65,536 tokens (up to 1,048,576 tokens) on GenerateContent , set max_output_tokens greater than 65,536 so the Google Gen AI SDK continues automatically across requests (or handle continuation_token in your own REST loop). Replace the reasoning budget parameter : Replace thinking_budget and MINIMAL with thinking_level set to LOW , MEDIUM (default on gemini-4-argon ), or HIGH (default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive ). Remove explicit caching and front-load static prompt content (6,144 tokens or more) for automatic implicit caching. Remove parameters that have no effect or aren't supported : Remove temperature , top_p , and top_k , which are ignored. Remove candidate_count , frequency_penalty , and presence_penalty . Remove any prefilled model turns from conversation histories. Summary checklist for developers Target model ID: gemini-4-argon (or gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive for Fairwind-approved projects), and upgrade to the latest Google Gen AI SDK (Python google-genai >= 2.30.1 , JS @google/genai >= 2.29.1 , Go >= 1.74.0 , Java >= 1.77.0 , .NET >= 1.26.0 , Kotlin >= 1.6.0 ) Location: global , us , or eu Budget for a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit and a 65,536-token single-request output cap (32,768 tokens for non-streaming direct HTTP calls), or set max_output_tokens up to 1,048,576 on GenerateContent for long decodes. Use thinking_level ( MEDIUM by default on gemini-4-argon , HIGH by default on gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive ; valid values: LOW , MEDIUM , HIGH ). Remove thinking_budget and MINIMAL . Remove the following parameters: frequency_penalty , presence_penalty , candidate_count , temperature , top_p , and top_k . Remove any prefilled model turns from multi-turn chat request histories. Remove explicit caching calls, and put static prompt content (6,144 tokens or more) first for implicit caching. Known issues Long decodes on GenerateContent require v1beta1 : Long decoding ( continuation_token ) on the GenerateContent API ( generateContent and streamGenerateContent ) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1 ). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is set in http_options ; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path. AI Quests invites students ages 11 to 14 to step into the shoes of Google researchers to tackle some of humanity’s biggest challenges. The quest is inspired by over a decade of our research in connectomics: the science of mapping neural networks in the brain. Upon completion of the quest, students hear from two researchers behind our real-world breakthroughs, including the recent mapping of the complete fruit fly brain, the largest brain map by number of neurons to date. Using tokens 3 as the new benchmark for the AI economy, the report projects that growing confidence in agentic commerce will drive a 60-fold surge in regional AI usage over the next five years. Here are the three key takeaways from this year's e-Conomy SEA 2026 report: 1. AI is sustaining growth in every sector. Across the digital economy, AI is reshaping how people live, shop, and move. E-commerce ($226B GMV, +18% YoY) anchors this shift, as shoppers use multimodal discovery and in-app assistants to confidently navigate complex purchases. These personalized experiences organically drive 10% higher conversions and order volume uplifts as large as 75%. In online travel ($59B GMV, +10% YoY), traditional search engines remain the top platform people use to plan travel, while generative AI has overtaken social media to become the second-most used tool for organizing complex itineraries. Online media ($44B revenue, +22% YoY) is personalizing content feeds and connecting audiences with more relevant ads, yielding a 10 to 20% quality engagement uplift as commerce media becomes a $4 billion market. Mobility and food delivery ($40B GMV, +15% YoY) saves consumers time via predictive suggestions, smarter routing, and AI-powered offerings like pooled rides, fueling healthy transactional growth. Finally, digital financial services ($1,650B GTV, +16% YoY) help consumers with real-time fraud detection, broader credit access, and personalized financial recommendations that complement human advice, alongside Singapore’s regional leadership in digital wealth platforms. 2. Consumer trust will help unlock the era of agentic commerce. Digital automation is already well established across the region, where 72% of users rely on everyday features like price tracking. This familiarity is clearing the runway for agentic commerce, with 75% expressing willingness to let AI agents autonomously compare prices and complete transactions on their behalf. This momentum is rooted in regional optimism: people in Southeast Asia view AI as a net benefit to society, with 62% reporting greater trust in AI tools today than a year ago. Driven by proven track records (56%), rising familiarity (55%), and output accuracy (53%), this trust signals a clear runway for deeper platform integration. To feel comfortable using new agentic capabilities, users expect clarity and guardrails, including robust privacy safeguards (44%), transparent information on what AI can and cannot do (36%), and the ability to reverse agentic transactions (30%). 3. Four major areas must adapt to enable AI adoption. To support a projected 60-fold increase in regional AI usage by 2030, the region's broader digital ecosystem must systematically evolve across four critical conditions: Accelerated agentic adoption and sustainable economics: Businesses need to move beyond using AI to answer single questions and start using it to help complete multi-step tasks from start to finish, backed by strong privacy safeguards and clear safety rules. At the same time, running AI models must keep getting more affordable and deliver clear, practical value, so businesses of all sizes can adopt the technology sustainably. Scaled physical infrastructure : Physical expansion must rapidly keep pace with soaring compute demand. Meeting this trajectory requires a ~3x expansion in data center capacity over the next five years, with AI workloads capturing a dominant share of total infrastructure. Strict model and energy efficiency : National frameworks, such as Singapore’s binding Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) rules under the Digital Infrastructure Bill, must guide next-generation facilities, paired with expanded clean energy access like Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS) model. Unified regional governance : Anchoring this trajectory, the upcoming ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) in November 2026 will establish the world's first region-wide digital trade pact, providing a framework that can unlock further growth in the Southeast Asia digital economy.
